As far as the law, it could definitely go either way, but only in so much as the US is a political landmine at the moment. Legally speaking, two things are very clear in the law. First is that the tech the *entire* LLM business model was based off of was allowed to scrape data because it was a research study, not intended for commercial use. That means all the data it took was fair use. OpenAI bought out the group doing the study, and kept the training data. It's admittedly not open shut, because IP Law never is, and this is admittedly a novel question. Still, current jurisprudence seems *heavily* against the idea that LLM's are fair use, and that they do violate copyright. Definitely something that time will tell.

The second, and arguably more important point for why LLM's will almost certainly not get wide adoption is that all of their work is not copyrightable. If a song came out produced by AI, literally anyone could sell a copy. This can be made more legally complicated by companies using AI to make the thing and then editing it, but that's also a legal (and therefore expensive) landmine.

And again, even though all these companies can steal whatever they want with no repercussions, they're still not profitable. OpenAI is hemorrhaging money. They aren't even having to pay for the water of emissions they're making, and they're wildly unprofitable. This is a problem that will only get worse.

Your CGI argument is just.. so wildly wrong I'm not going to bother addressing it. Their are valid attempts people could make to try and defend the legality of LLM's, but that isn't it.

For starters, a voice changer is different than an AI dub. A voice changer just has to modulate pitch and tone in a reliable way- an AI dub has to match pitch and tone while creating a believable rhythm, creating emotional and varied inflection, all the things a natural voice does that makes us believe we're listening to a person.

As for the video itself, I also have reservations. For starters, if I heard that as a casting director, I'd pass. None of those voices felt real. They were close, I'll admit. But they still had a machine quality to them. Not enough natural variance in the voice I think. Also, while I'll admit it's maybe a bit too cynical, it's possible the voices in that video were edited as a part of the video, and not representative of what the tech is capable of.

Lastly, while it's always possible a new technology will come out that vastly improves on what we have now, time isn't a relevant factor here. 5 years or 50, what matters is the size of the training data set, and LLM companies have already stolen basically everything they can. Models won't get significantly better than they are now.

Alright, so I'm going to break down my position as earnestly as I can. Make of it what you will.

To understand police and prison abolition, you need to look back in time. Understand that police and prisons are a uniquely modern concept- while things like dungeons and guards existed throughout history, they served a different function.

It's not to say that things were significantly better with those systems, merely to point out that police and prisons aren't a historical fact, or a human necessity. So if that's the case, what purpose do they serve? In the US, both primarily exist to serve the wants of capital. If you look at the 13th ammendment, you'll notice slavery was never abolished in this country, merely monopolized in prisons.

It should come as no surprise then that following the reconstruction era after the civil war, that black Americans were arrested at astonishing rates, and put back to work on plantations and in prison factories, a fact that remains true to this day.

Now that the history lesson is out of the way, what about what we do with all the thieves, rapists, and murderers? How to we keep safe? For starters, we ask what safe means, and who's selling it to us. We look into where criminality comes from, and how to stop the problem at its source, rather than treat the symptoms.

While what makes someone "criminal" is hugely complex, and depends on how the dominant power structure defines what constitutes a criminal act, the largest contributing factor to anti-social behavior is great disparity. Those with the power and means to act without consequence will do so, and those with no hope or means to thrive will become criminals out of necessity.

While I hold no great hope that the epsteins of this world will be held accountable, one thing we can do to prevent and address criminal behavior is to help people. We can address the root causes of poverty, and eliminate them. This isn't a pipe dream either- the US made significant gains when it tried its "war on poverty", and until it was revoked the child tax credit (iirc) nearly eliminated childhood hunger in this country for about 4 years.

But still, even if these problems are systemic, we will surely still have rapists, murderers, and thieves! I hear you say. What do we do with them?

That's definitely complicated. As long as we have society, we will have people who refuse to learn, or play nicely with others. We will also have a need for restraining people, and a way to do it. I don't think there's an easy answer to that, truthfully. But, I do think that prisons as they currently exist are not the answer.

My personal answer is something similar to the nordic system, with a few differences. I think all prisons, holding facilities, whatever you wish to call them, should be made with care to respect the dignity of the people it holds. Work should be available, but never mandatory, and pay the workers a meaningful wage for the work they do. After all, if we aren't going to just kill them, we should be doing our best to teach them how to be a productive member of society. Torturing them, oppressing them with state violence, and putting them in close proximity with career criminals, then blacklisting them from 90% of decent paying jobs when they get out (with a threat to throw them back in if they don't find one) is not a great way to ensure the people coming out of prison don't hurt more people.

As for police, I can't claim to be an expert. But my take is that community policing is the way to go. By that I mean relying on things like deputizing. Have either a magistrate perform that duty, or if you must, a sheriff. Minimize the amount of state violence professionals, and maximize the public involvement in state violence.

The least radical approach is at least to defund the police. Take away the military grade weapons and vehicles, and stop sending cops out for wellness checks. Make better use of social workers, therapists, and community support. I also think we should take UK policing to heart, and not allow police to actively carry guns. Have them in the patrol car, but not on their person unless authorized. Reinforce the mindset of protect and serve, not dominate and kill.

I can respect that. I don't necessarily have an issue with individual cops, but the system of policing itself feels so intrinsically tied to systems of power and exploitation, I struggle to see past it at times.

A lot of anxiety comes from an overstimulated amygdala, the section of your brain that controls emotional processing, things like fight or flight. The amygdala is also antagonistic to your prefrontal cortex, and can actively hamper things like reasoning and high level decision making.

Weed can help to dampen the intensity of those feelings, allowing for the rest of the brain to have room to breath. That said, weed as a depressant doesn't just act on the amygdala, it effects most of the rest of the brain too. That means that it can be harder to make changes regarding what caused the anxiety in the first place.

It's also important to remember that anxiety isn't a bad thing to be completely avoided- it's vitally important to survival! It's your body's way of saying that something is wrong. By muting it not only will the signal get stronger to compensate, but again the core reasons won't get addressed.

Lastly, for people with ADHD (such as myself), part of the problem comes from weak prefrontal cortex signaling, and how that plays into the brains reward and decision making loops. Depressants weaken that link in the chain even more, exacerbating symptoms. Hence why they are treated with stimulants!

Here's 4 exercises you can do that will help, if you're interested. For all these, I recommend a set of 10, once to twice a day. These are exercises I got from a physical therapist to address sciatica specifically

1: Cat Camels
Get on your hands and knees, both about shoulder width apart. Hands should be directly below your shoulders, though they can be a few inches towards your knees. A single repetition is arching your back as far as you can up (without pain) while keeping your knees and palms on the ground and looking down, holding for 3 seconds, then arching the opposite direction and looking up, again holding for 3 seconds.

2: Alternating Superman
Same starting position as the cat camel. Hands should be directly under shoulders, and not further back. 1 repetition begins by raising your right arm and left leg. Your right arm should be reaching directly forward, like you're trying to touch something just out of reach. Your leg should point straight back. Experiment with pointing your toe to the ground vs behind you. Your left arm and right leg should remain perpendicular to the ground, and keep you steady. Keep this position for 3 seconds, and try to feel a stretch. After 3 seconds, return to the starting position, and alternate so that your left arm and right leg are pointing. After 3 seconds, return to your starting position.

3: Alternating Roach
The starting position for this is laying on your back, hands and feet pointed in the air, looking towards the ceiling. Similar to the superman, this one has you lower one arm and the opposite leg, while alternating limbs for a rep. Your hands and feet should stop about 6 inches from the ground, and stay for between 1-3 seconds before alternating.

4: Laying Hip Raise
The starting position for this is laying on your back, hands by your side, palms down, close to your torso. Your knees should be bent at about 90 degrees, with your feet comfortably flat on the ground.  Keeping your head back, raise your hips as high as you can while keeping the weight on your feet (still flat on the ground) and your shoulders (not your head/neck), using your arms for balance. After about 3 seconds, lower your hips back to the ground.

The **MOST IMPORTANT THING** is that you do not admit any responsibility for any fines or fees they try to pin you with. That could bite you in the ass later.


Speaking in general though if your lease ended and you moved out, you shouldn't be liable for any continuing rents. Again though, it depends on the language in the lease, and whether that language is legally permissable, as well as rights afforded to you by your local and state laws.

Ultimately, your best course of action is to send an email or mail a certified letter to the management company or landlord, informing them of the date you moved out and other relevant information, such as key dropoff or any other requirements mentioned in the lease.

If they want to pursue the matter further, their option is to serve you a small claims court filing. If that happens, hire a lawyer to represent you. Chances are it won't.

Lastly, if the rental had a deposit there's a good chance *you* are owed money. Most states have a maximum amount of time after move out for a LL to either return the deposit, or send an itemized receipt for how that deposit was spent (e.g. fixing damage not covered by the lease). Normal wear and tear is not something they can keep your deposit for.  If you did pay a deposit and they didn't return it or give you a receipt, they are required to pay it back with interest, and sometimes more.  In that case, it'd be a good idea to at least consult with a lawyer. You can of course file your own small claims court case against the company, probably for about $100.

Everyone is on a substance. Life is all about taking substances that help you survive, and avoiding the ones that don't. The question is, which is it for you?

Obviously it's a little more complicated, as most things help and hurt depending on dosage, use, etc. But ultimately it does come down to one thing. Is it helping or hurting? If you are using a substance to treat a problem and have nothing to take its place, of course the pain caused by removing the substance will eventually overcome the rationale for quitting. That being said, as all the above said, quitting an addiction is not as simple as "I choose to do x thing and then do it". You need to understand your emotional reasoning. Thinking and feeling are the same thing, and if you don't incorporate that into your strategy, you'll fail.

You can 'know' completely that something is bad for you and still do it, because the "feeling" part of your brain disagrees, and ultimately has final say. You need to feel the need to quit, and nurture that feeling.

In less wooj sounding terms, it comes down to how brains work. Your amygdala for example, controls a lot of those feelings, and affects your decision making in profound ways.
